updates.note: The primary Science article (DOI 10.1126/science.aec2657; PMID 42561074; published 2026-08-06) reports the first generative design of complete bacteriophage genomes using genome language models and experimental testing of 16 viable phages. The bioRxiv version (DOI 10.1101/2025.09.12.675911) and Arc Institute's official technical explainer provide the source history and describe the human-led fine-tuning, prompting, screening, genome assembly, host-range testing, and biosafety procedures. This is enough evidence for public review as an AI-assisted genome-design result; independent replication, broader host-range limits, and external confirmation of safety claims remain open.
updates.title: AI-designed bacteriophage genomes yield 16 viable phages
updates.summary: Genome language models Evo 1 and Evo 2 generated complete bacteriophage genomes using ΦX174 as a design template. Laboratory testing yielded 16 viable phages with diverse fitness profiles; one was characterized by cryo-electron microscopy and a generated-phage cocktail overcame ΦX174-resistant E. coli strains in laboratory testing.
updates.aiSystem: Evo 1 and Evo 2 genome language models
updates.whyItMatters: The study demonstrates that genome language models can generate genetically novel bacteriophages that function in laboratory hosts, creating a testable route for synthetic phage design; therapeutic use and broader host-range claims remain open.
updates.aiRole: Evo 1 and Evo 2 generated candidate whole-genome sequences and helped explore sequence space; researchers chose the ΦX174 template, fine-tuned and prompted the models, screened 285 designs, assembled and tested the genomes, characterized the 16 functional phages, and interpreted the host-range and biosafety experiments.
updates.verificationNote: The Science/PubMed primary record reports 16 viable phages with laboratory fitness testing, cryo-electron microscopy of a generated capsid protein, and resistance experiments in E. coli. The Arc Institute technical explainer reports 285 designs screened, restricted tropism to non-pathogenic laboratory E. coli hosts, and dedicated containment procedures. The authors' safety claim is recorded as source-reported rather than independently established. Crossref shows no update relation, and the PMID-specific NCBI notice search found no retraction, erratum, expression-of-concern, or correction signal.
